description: Visconti and Sforza signoria (1395–1535) that dominated the Po plain and the Alpine passes into northern Italy; its formidable army, sophisticated diplomacy, and cultural patronage, Bramante, Leonardo, Filarete, made it one of the five great powers of the Italian state system before French and Spanish intervention ended its independence.

temporal.notes: Visconti and then Sforza; major Italian power

lifecycle_phases.description: Gian Galeazzo Visconti purchases the ducal title (1395) and nearly unifies northern Italy before his death of plague (1402). His successors struggle with French, Venetian, and Florentine pressure. The last male Visconti dies (1447); a brief Ambrosian Republic collapses. The mercenary captain Francesco Sforza marries the last Visconti's illegitimate daughter and conquers Milan (1450).

Francesco Sforza and his son Ludovico 'il Moro' (1481–1499) make Milan the greatest Renaissance court in Italy, patronizing Leonardo da Vinci, Bramante, and dozens of scholars. Ludovico's invitation to Charles VIII of France (1494) to invade Italy, to use the French as leverage against Naples, triggers the Italian Wars. Louis XII of France deposes Ludovico (1499), ending the Sforza duchy temporarily.

rise_factors.description: The Duchy's silk industry, armor workshops, and Alpine trade routes made Milan the most economically productive state in northern Italy; the Sforza's patronage of engineers (Leonardo da Vinci designed canals and fortifications) maximized the economic potential of the region

Milan commanded the Po Valley trade routes connecting the Alps to the Adriatic; control of Alpine passes (Simplon, St. Gotthard, Brenner approaches) gave Milan customs revenues from the entire north-south trade axis

Milan's arms industry produced the finest plate armor in Europe; Milanese smiths supplied knights from England to Byzantium; the city's wealth funded mercenary condottieri armies that shaped Italian politics

Milan's armorer guilds produced the finest plate armor in Europe, making the duchy a major export center and giving its rulers enormous war revenues from sales to French, Burgundian, and German knights.
The Visconti family consolidated control over all of Lombardy through military conquest and marriage alliances in the 14th century, creating a centralized duchy from previously fragmented communes.

decline_factors.description: Ludovico Sforza's invitation to Charles VIII to invade Italy (1494) unleashed the Italian Wars that Milan could not control; the French claim to Milan through the Visconti inheritance brought overwhelming external military force against which the duchy had no answer

French invasion of Italy (1494) led by Charles VIII and subsequent Habsburg-Valois wars turned northern Italy into a battlefield; Milan changed hands repeatedly between France and Spain, ultimately becoming a Spanish possession (1535)
Visconti line extinction (1447) and the Sforza usurpation created legitimacy questions exploited by foreign powers; French claims through Valentina Visconti provided pretext for the 1494 invasion
The Italian Wars (1494–1559) saw Milan become the central battlefield between French Valois and Habsburg forces, repeatedly changing hands and devastating urban and agricultural infrastructure.
The extinction of the Sforza male line in 1535 allowed Charles V to incorporate Milan as a Habsburg imperial fief, ending its status as an independent Italian signoria.
